single-binary outbound mail server

Mail delivery.
Not a mail stack.

outboxd gives applications one focused SMTP server for reliable outbound email — authenticated submission, durable queues, direct MX delivery, DKIM, DNS guidance, TLS and even OpenPGP/MIME signing and recipient encryption when you configure the keys.

the whole path

Your app submits mail. outboxd handles the annoying parts.

It is deliberately not an IMAP server, webmail client or inbound filtering stack. It does one job: take mail from trusted applications and get it delivered correctly.

01 / SUBMIT

your application

Use ordinary authenticated SMTP on 587 with STARTTLS or 465 with implicit TLS.

→
02 / PROCESS

outboxd

Authenticate, canonicalize, optionally OpenPGP-sign/encrypt, DKIM-sign, queue and retry from one daemon.

→
03 / DELIVER

recipient MX

Resolve the recipient domain and deliver directly over SMTP on port 25 — no relay service required.

batteries included

Almost everything outbound mail asks you to get right.

The point is not to recreate Postfix plus a pile of sidecars. The point is to make the common application-mail setup small, explicit and understandable.

MX

Direct delivery

Resolve recipient MX records and deliver straight to destination servers, with a durable on-disk queue in between.

One configuration

One binary, one private data directory and one commented configuration file instead of a multi-service mail stack.

GOSINGLE BINARYSYSTEMD
not an afterthought

OpenPGP support all the way through the message pipeline.

Configure signing per sender and recipient keys for encryption. outboxd builds the final MIME variant first, then applies DKIM last so the message that leaves the queue is exactly what was authenticated.

Signed when required. Encrypted when possible — or required.

Sender identities can require OpenPGP/MIME signing. Recipient keys are operator-supplied and matched to exact addresses; configured recipients are encrypted rather than silently falling back to plaintext.

dns without guesswork

Generate the records. Publish them. Check the deployment.

outboxd prints the deployment information around your configured hostname, domain and key material, so the last mile is copying records into your DNS provider rather than reconstructing them by hand.

Authentication is part of the setup, not a later checklist.

DKIM is generated from the actual provisioned key. SPF, DMARC and TLS-RPT guidance is emitted alongside it, with optional OPENPGPKEY records when enabled.

Amail203.0.113.10
TXT@v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.10 -all
TXT_dmarcv=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com
TXToutboxd._domainkeyv=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqh…
TXT_smtp._tlsv=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:tlsrpt@example.com
TYPE61<hash>._openpgpkey\# … optional OPENPGPKEY RDATA
install

One daemon. One setup.

The guided installer sets up the Linux service layout, downloads and verifies the release, provisions the essentials and walks through DNS output.

01
InstallRun the guided Linux installer or unpack a release yourself.
02
ConfigureSet hostname, sending domain, public IP, TLS and SMTP users.
03
ProvisionCreate the queue, private state and create-once DKIM material.
04
Publish + checkCopy the generated DNS guidance, run the deployment checks and start the service.
$ curl -fsSL https://src.ws2.sh/outboxd/install.sh | sh

Network-delivered root installer: inspect the script before running it. Prefer release archives if you want a fully manual path.

config.yml
minimal
server:
  hostname: mail.example.com
  domain: example.com
  data_directory: /opt/outboxd/data

tls:
  mode: files
  certificate_file: /opt/outboxd/data/tls/fullchain.pem
  private_key_file: /opt/outboxd/data/tls/privkey.pem

dns:
  public_ipv4: 203.0.113.10
